articles.title: Time to Plan Your Nicest Vacation Yet! Here’s Your Guide to All of Reader’s Digest’s Nicest Places in America Winners

阿什维尔融合了大城市的创造力与小镇的魅力，这种独特的结合使其成为美国最友好城市的2025年冠军。这座坐落于蓝岭山脉的小城以其文化、怪癖和包容性吸引着游客，尤其是那些喜爱艺术、美食和本地风情的旅行者。沿着法国广河的艺术区是城市的创意中心，这里有许多艺术家和工匠的工作室和画廊，原本是工业建筑。游客可以在这里漫步，观看艺术家们创作，甚至参与手工制作课程。阿什维尔还拥有多家詹姆斯比尔奖获奖餐厅，如Cúrate酒吧和Chai Pani，这些餐厅不仅提供美味食物，也展现了社区精神。2024年9月，飓风海伦袭击该地区后，Chai Pani的骨干团队迅速行动，为数百名邻居提供了三明治。这种社区互助精神使得阿什维尔的酒厂、独立商店和画廊探索变得更加特别。推荐住宿：The Foundry酒店位于一座改建的钢铁工厂内，保留了许多原始工业细节，如裸露的砖墙，位于The Block社区，这是城市历史上的黑人社区，距离市中心的商店、餐厅和景点仅几步之遥。 普罗沃位于犹他州，周边环绕着瓦萨奇山脉，提供多种户外活动。这座海拔较高的城市是布里戈姆扬大学所在地，拥有约3.5万名学生，充满青春活力，同时也有强烈的社区精神和志愿服务文化。游客可以选择爬Y山（Y山）的陡峭小径，到达山顶后可以看到普罗沃和犹他湖的全景。对于轻松出行，可以沿着普罗河畔的平坦步道散步或骑自行车。秋季，阿尔派恩环路风景大道的森林景色非常壮观，游客可以在此停留远足、野餐或参观提姆潘诺戈斯洞国家纪念馆。冬季，普罗沃也是滑雪和单板滑雪的便利起点，附近的日舞山度假村是理想选择。推荐住宿：位于市中心的Hines豪宅是一座维多利亚式豪宅，由Richard Kletting设计，他也是犹他州议会大厦的设计师。这座建筑保留了许多时期特色，距离市中心的商店和景点步行可达。 布法罗位于纽约州上州，是湖伊利湖畔人口近30万的城市，暖和的天气使其成为理想的度假胜地。友好的氛围在350英亩的德拉维尔公园（Hoyt湖）展现得淋漓尽致。夏季，公园内的日本花园、玫瑰园以及每年免费的戈德纳公园莎士比亚戏剧节都充满活力。当然，NFL足球队水牛城比尔队是城市性格的重要组成部分。秋季，球迷可以在新建的Highmark体育场（Orchard Park）感受水牛城比尔文化。球迷的热情从赛前派对到比赛日场内的海洋蓝和红色可见一斑。此外，科学体育场是布法罗科学博物馆的新常设展览，游客可以在这里探索足球和科学背后的故事，甚至可以在主播桌前录制自己的体育节目。推荐住宿：Richardson酒店位于19世纪精神疗养院旧址，是国家历史地标，其园林由景观设计师Frederick Law Olmsted和Calvert Vaux设计，仍然展示着他们的宏伟愿景。 库尔特维尔是加州北部的一座小镇，人口仅118人，但拥有丰富的历史和自然资源。这座前金矿城镇是通往约塞米蒂国家公园的重要途径，现存有几座保存完好的金矿时代建筑，如Sun Sun Wo Co.，曾是库尔特维尔唐人街的一部分。游客可以在北马里波萨县历史中心体验金洗，并看到Whistling Billy，一辆八吨重的Porter机车，曾用于运输附近矿山的矿石。推荐住宿：Vacation Station是一辆改造成独特住宿的1964年货运火车车厢，适合体验库尔特维尔的独特魅力。更大的团体可以考虑约塞米蒂天堂旅店，这是一家位于城镇外的床早餐式旅店。 科达克是田纳西州塞维尔县的一个小镇，地理位置优越，距离东田纳西州最受欢迎的景点仅15-25英里。皮奇福格是烟雾山脉的娱乐中心，拥有多莉·帕顿的多莉伍德主题公园和多种现场音乐和晚宴表演。盖特林堡是大烟雾山国家公园的山地度假小镇，距离科达克约15英里。诺克斯维尔以其餐厅、博物馆和历史街区闻名，距离科达克约20英里。对于自然爱好者，烟雾山脉的风景驱动和800多英里的步道距离科达克约25英里，是美国参观人数最多的国家公园，非常适合日游。推荐住宿：位于科达克的Quality Inn Interstate在2021年被《读者文摘》评为美国最友好地方，主人Sean Patel在2020年圣诞夜前的大暴风雪中为当地居民提供了折扣房间，非常适合探索周边景点，如多莉伍德和烟雾山脉。 密歇根州南部的布坎南距离芝加哥仅90分钟车程，是一个小而充满活力的城市。2020年，《读者文摘》将其评为美国最友好城市，以表彰居民在抗击种族不公和战胜新冠肺炎疫情方面的团结精神。这座只有4000多人的城市提供了许多超乎想象的活动。市中心的前街林立着独立商店、咖啡馆和餐厅。The Common是社区聚集地，举办音乐会、节日、农贸市场等活动。周围的自然环境也非常迷人，McCoy Creek Trail是一条约4英里的小径，穿过森林和水域，适合步行或骑自行车。对于想品尝本地酒和精酿啤酒的游客，Hickory Creek Winery和River Saint Joe农场精酿啤酒厂是不错的选择。推荐住宿：Morris Estate位于距离市中心约5英里的600英亩河畔乡村，提供套房、小木屋和美丽的景色。该庄园曾是E.M. Morris家族的农场和度假地，他们是当地慈善家和前诺特丹大学学生，对该地区有着重要影响。 俄亥俄州东北部的哥伦比纳是一个全年都充满节日氛围的城市。每年9月，全城举办哥伦比纳街头节，这是一个长期传统，让邻居们相互认识并为当地美国退伍军人协会筹款。游客可以享受游乐设施、美食、音乐和游行。尽管名字如此，哥伦比纳距离克利夫兰比哥伦布更近，甚至距离坎顿（NFL足球名人堂所在地）更近。足球迷可以观看布朗队比赛或前往名人堂，然后在附近的人文风情床早餐式旅店过夜。或者，可以前往约30分钟车程的杨斯敦，了解该地区丰富的钢铁厂历史。秋季，爱好古董和复古的人可以参加Shaker Woods的古董市集。冬季，当地居民聚集庆祝“圣诞欢乐灯光节”，配有饼干和热巧克力。春夏季，户外活动如6月的哥伦比纳葡萄酒节和7月4日的烟花表演让人心驰神往。推荐住宿：距离哥伦比纳约30分钟车程的Chapel Valley Estate是一座改建的农场，位于匹兹堡郊外的9英亩宁静乡村，2003年全面翻新，保留了许多原始石墙，为访客提供老世界的魅力。 诺克斯维尔是一个值得一游的城市，推荐从Yassin's Falafel House开始，该餐厅在2018年被《读者文摘》评为美国最友好地方。餐厅主人Yassin Terou是一名叙利亚难民，在诺克斯维尔餐饮界占据了一席之地，使餐厅成为所有顾客的安全而真诚的社区。然后，前往市中心，参观太阳球的观景台，这是1982年诺克斯维尔世界博览会的象征。旁边是一个独一无二的礼物，一座高10英尺、重1,200磅的巨型魔方方块，由匈牙利赠送，以纪念魔方的诞生地。对于更加可爱和亲切的体验，可以前往诺克斯维尔动物园，这里是世界上出生最多红熊猫的动物园，因此诺克斯维尔被誉为“世界红熊猫之都”。推荐住宿：Oliver酒店坐落在诺克斯维尔的市场广场上的一座19世纪的面包房内，提供28间客房，为游客提供自行车探索历史悠久的城市，或呆在酒店内，参观Peter Kern图书馆酒吧，这是一个以文学为主题的秘密酒吧。 田纳西州纳什维尔都市区以东23英里处的加拉廷是一座充满活力的城市。尽管正在迅速发展，但仍保留了小镇的特色，使其成为《读者文摘》2017年美国最友好地方的首个获奖城市。 The historic downtown is a good place to get to know Gallatin, starting with stops in its many locally owned shops and restaurants clustered around the courthouse square. Pay a visit to the elegant 1842 Greek Revival mansion Rose Mont, then stop at the Sumner County Museum to learn more about the people and events that shaped the region. The great outdoors are an important part of life here too. Spend a day boating and fishing on Old Hickory Lake, or trade the water for the hiking trails of Bledsoe Creek State Park. Where to stay: A night at the four-bedroom, four-bathroom Historic Stonewall is one of Gallatin’s most unique and storied stays. The nearly 200-year-old property has lived many lives, from a doctor’s home and boys’ dormitory to a private family residence. Today, it’s a historic property managed by the Sumner County Museum, which books it for overnight stays. 2025 winner: Asheville, North Carolina

Asheville has the perfect blend of big-city creativity and small-town charm. Cultured, quirky and welcoming, this small city in the Blue Ridge Mountains—our 2025 Nicest Place in America winner—is especially appealing to travelers who like their sightseeing with a heaping side of interesting art, delicious food and plenty of local character.

The River Arts District, along the French Broad River, is the city’s creative quarter. Here, artists and craftspeople, from ironworkers and painters to potters and glassblowers, have studios and galleries in former industrial buildings. It’s an area made for spending a day getting lost, watching artists at work or joining a hands-on class to make art of your own.

The city is also home to many James Beard Award–winning restaurants, including Cúrate Bar de Tapas and Chai Pani. These restaurants serve more than just great food—they offer a window into the community spirit that makes Asheville so special. After Hurricane Helene devastated the region in September 2024, many local restaurants sprang into action—including Indian street-food restaurant Chai Pani, where a skeleton crew wrapped sandwiches to feed hundreds of neighbors.

That’s just one of the many stories that explain why exploring Asheville’s many breweries, independent shops and galleries—or even visiting the Biltmore, the impressive Vanderbilt estate just outside downtown—feels more special than a typical getaway.

Where to stay: Boutique property The Foundry Hotel occupies a restored former steel foundry, and it features exposed brick and other original industrial details throughout. Located in The Block, the city’s historically Black neighborhood, the hotel is also just steps from downtown shops, restaurants and attractions.

2024 winner: Provo, Utah

I’ve passed through Provo, Utah, many times, and it’s the kind of place where you can spend a morning hiking through the surrounding Wasatch Mountains and be back in town for lunch. Its location makes it especially appealing for outdoor enthusiasts, since it has so many options for hikers, bikers, anglers, climbers and more, all close at hand.

Home to Brigham Young University and some 35,000 students, Provo has the unmistakable atmosphere and energy of a college town, but also a strong sense of community and a culture of volunteerism.

A trip to the high-altitude city might include a steep hike on the trails of Y Mountain. Once you reach the giant white Y, which was created by university students in the early 20th century, you’ll be rewarded with panoramic views of Provo and Utah Lake. For an easier outing, take a walk or bike ride along the paved parkway beside the Provo River, which winds into scenic Provo Canyon.

Autumn turns crisp and more than a little magical in this part of Utah. The season brings the forests along the Alpine Loop Scenic Byway to vivid life, and there are plenty of opportunities to stop for a brisk hike, cozy picnic or worthwhile visit to Timpanogos Cave National Monument. When the snow starts falling, Provo is also a convenient launching point for skiing and snowboarding at nearby Sundance Mountain Resort.

Where to stay: For a dose of history, book a room at the eight-suite Hines Mansion, a Victorian-era mansion in downtown Provo designed by Richard Kletting, the architect behind the Utah State Capitol. Filled with character and original period details, it’s within walking distance of many of downtown Provo’s most interesting shops and stops.

Book Now

2023 winner: Buffalo, New York

In Upstate New York, warmer weather makes Buffalo, a city of nearly 300,000 people on the shores of Lake Erie, a pretty compelling getaway. The friendly vibe in the City of Good Neighbors is on full display in the 350-acre Delaware Park on Hoyt Lake. Often called the city’s Central Park, the centerpiece of Frederick Law Olmsted’s pioneering park system comes alive in summer, from the Japanese Garden and Rose Garden to Shakespeare in Delaware Park, the annual free outdoor theater tradition.

Of course, the NFL’s Buffalo Bills are woven into the city’s personality. In the fall, football fans can experience the city’s passionate Bills culture at the brand-new Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park. Pride in the hometown team is palpable, from the tailgating parties to the sea of blue and red that fills the stadium on game days.

And now, fans can get an inside look at the sport at Science Stadium, a new permanent exhibition at the Buffalo Museum of Science. The interactive, hands-on experience explores football and the science behind it, and gives fans the chance to record their own highlight-reel sportscast from an anchor desk.

Where to stay: The Richardson Hotel, in a former 19th-century mental health treatment complex, is now a National Historic Landmark. Its grounds were designed by landscape architects Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, and the property still showcases their grand vision of architecture and green space on the Richardson Olmsted Campus.

Book Now

2022 winner: Coulterville, California

On a recent trip through Northern California, I drove along roads that wound past rolling fields, sprawling ranches and wide-open spaces before reaching tiny Coulterville, a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it town in Northern California. With just 118 residents, according to the latest official census, the former Gold Rush town is worth slowing down for. In a region where wildfires can rage out of control, threatening livelihoods, the people who call Coulterville home have learned they can rely on one another.

This rugged corner in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada gets far less attention than San Francisco, about 140 miles to the west, but Coulterville was once a thriving gold-mining mecca and a major stop on the way to another national treasure, Yosemite—which is the reason I stumbled upon the tiny town.

Today, it has a handful of preserved Gold Rush–era buildings lining Main Street, like the Sun Sun Wo Co., a former Chinese mercantile that was part of Coulterville’s Chinatown. Stop at the Northern Mariposa County History Center for a bit of on-site gold panning and to see Whistling Billy, an eight-ton Porter locomotive once used to haul ore from nearby mines.

Where to stay: For a unique taste of Coulterville, spend the night in a 1964 boxcar and caboose at Vacation Station, a decommissioned train converted into one-of-a-kind lodging. Larger groups might consider the Yosemite Paradise Inn, a bed-and-breakfast just outside of town.

Book Now

2021 winner: Kodak, Tennessee

The tiny town of Kodak, in Sevier County, has a big and very convenient advantage: Its central location puts several of East Tennessee’s most visited attractions within easy reach.

Pigeon Forge, the entertainment hub of the Smokies and home to Dolly Parton’s Dollywood, as well as numerous live dinner and music shows, is about 15 miles away. The area around the iconic theme park will no doubt be hosting many events and tributes to the late singer and beloved philanthropist, so stop by if you’re in the area.

Gatlinburg, a mountain resort town and gateway to Great Smoky Mountains National Park, is a similar distance from Kodak. And Knoxville, with its restaurants, museums and historic neighborhoods, is about 20 miles west. For nature lovers, the scenic drives and 800-plus miles of trails of the Smokies are roughly 25 miles south, making the country’s most-visited national park an easy day trip.

Where to stay: The Quality Inn Interstate in Kodak was named Reader’s Digest‘s Nicest Place in America in 2021, so why not stay there? The proprietor, Sean Patel, an immigrant from India, offered locals rooms at a fraction of the usual rate when a major winter storm on Christmas Eve 2020 left many in the area without power. The conveniently located property is a great base for exploring the surrounding sites, including Dollywood and the Smoky Mountains.

Book Now

2020 winner: Buchanan, Michigan

In southwest Michigan, the small city of Buchanan is about 90 minutes from Chicago—but a world away. In 2020, Reader’s Digest named the Midwestern city its Nicest Place in America, recognizing how residents here came together that year to fight racial injustice and overcome the coronavirus pandemic.

More than six years later, the town of just over 4,000 residents remains a genuinely appealing and easy escape, and there’s much more to do than its small size might suggest. Downtown, Front Street is lined with independent shops, cafes and restaurants. The Common, a community gathering place, hosts concerts, festivals, farmers markets and other events that bring residents together.

The town is also surrounded by nature. The roughly four-mile McCoy Creek Trail winds through woods and along the water, making it a pleasant way to explore the area by foot or bike. For a taste of the region’s wine and craft-beverage scene, head to Hickory Creek Winery or River Saint Joe, a farmstead brewery.

Where to stay: Set on 600 acres of riverfront countryside about 5 miles from downtown Buchanan, the Morris Estate offers suites, cabins and plenty of scenic views. The estate was a farm and retreat for the family of E.M. Morris, a local philanthropist and former Notre Dame student whose influence can be heavily felt in the area. A darling vintage chapel, delicious dining and luxurious accommodations await you.

Book Now

2019 winner: Columbiana, Ohio

Columbiana, in northeastern Ohio, is a festive place to visit at any time of year. But each September, the city comes alive to celebrate the Columbiana Street Fair, a longstanding tradition that allows neighbors to meet neighbors and raises money for the local American Legion. The entire town (and anyone stopping by) can enjoy rides, food, music and a parade.

Despite its name, Columbiana is closer to Cleveland than Columbus—and even closer to Canton, home of the NFL’s Football Hall of Fame. Football fans can take in a Browns game or head to the Hall of Fame and then stay overnight at one of the area’s charming bed-and-breakfasts. Or you can head to Youngstown, just a half-hour away, to learn about the region’s rich steel-mill history.

Estate-sale buffs and other vintage hunters can browse Antiques in the Woods, an event held each fall just outside of town in the Shaker Woods. When cold weather arrives, locals gather for the Joy of Christmas Holiday Light Festival, complete with cookies and hot cocoa. Come spring and summer, the outdoors beckon with the Columbiana Wine Festival at Firestone Farms in June and a 4th of July fireworks display.

Where to stay: About a half-hour drive from Columbiana, Chapel Valley Estate is a renovated farmhouse turned warm and welcoming bed-and-breakfast set on 9 acres in the peaceful countryside outside of Pittsburgh. Completely redone in 2003, the estate features natural stone walls that were unearthed during the renovations, adding an old-world charm to any visit.

Book Now

2018 winner: Yassin’s Falafel House, Knoxville, Tennessee

There are many reasons to visit Knoxville, but start with a meal at Yassin’s Falafel House, named Reader’s Digest’s Nicest Place in America in 2018. The restaurant’s owner and operator, Yassin Terou, a Syrian refugee, has carved out a niche in the city’s food scene and made the restaurant a safe place and true community for everyone who walks through the door.

Then, head downtown and check out the observation deck at the Sunsphere, the hard-to-miss gold disco ball built for the World’s Fair when Knoxville hosted it in 1982. Right next door, you’ll find one of the world’s most unique gifts: a giant 10-foot-tall, 1,200-pound Rubik’s Cube, given to the city by Hungary, where the puzzle was born.

For something equally rare but a lot more cute and cuddly, check out Zoo Knoxville, which holds the distinction of being the birthplace of more red pandas than any other zoo in the world. In fact, the feat has earned Knoxville the nickname “The Red Panda Capital of the World.”

Where to stay: The 28-room Oliver Hotel occupies a restored 19th-century bakery right on Knoxville’s Market Square. The hotel provides bikes for guests to explore the historic city, but it’s a worthy destination itself for those who prefer to stay in and visit the on-site literary-themed speakeasy, Peter Kern Library.

Book Now

2017 winner: Gallatin, Tennessee

Once a farming community along the Cumberland River, Gallatin has grown into a thriving city in the Nashville metropolitan area. Just 23 miles northeast of the Tennessee capital, it’s growing rapidly while holding onto the small-town character that earned it the distinction of Reader’s Digest’s very first Nicest Places in America title in 2017.

The historic downtown is a good place to get to know Gallatin, starting with stops in its many locally owned shops and restaurants clustered around the courthouse square. Pay a visit to the elegant 1842 Greek Revival mansion Rose Mont, then stop at the Sumner County Museum to learn more about the people and events that shaped the region.

The great outdoors are an important part of life here too. Spend a day boating and fishing on Old Hickory Lake, or trade the water for the hiking trails of Bledsoe Creek State Park.

Where to stay: A night at the four-bedroom, four-bathroom Historic Stonewall is one of Gallatin’s most unique and storied stays. The nearly 200-year-old property has lived many lives, from a doctor’s home and boys’ dormitory to a private family residence. Today, it’s a historic property managed by the Sumner County Museum, which books it for overnight stays.

articles.title: Watch The Reader’s Digest Escalator Interview with Actor and Author Ke Huy Quan
articles.content: If anyone knows a thing or two about never saying die, it’s Ke Huy Quan. The actor first stole hearts as Short Round in Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom and Data in The Goonies, and then, after decades away from acting, he made the kind of Hollywood comeback that movies are made of with Everything Everywhere All at Once. His unforgettable turn as Waymond Wang earned him an Academy Award, Golden Globe and SAG Award for Best Supporting Actor, and in 2023, Time named him one of the 100 most influential people in the world. articles.title: 11 Ways to Turn Your Community into One of the Nicest Places in America
articles.content:
What makes your community a nice place to live? Is it feeling safe and secure, or having access to parks and services? Maybe it’s all about having your family close, or lots of opportunities for career advancement. A great place to live can be all of those things—and if you love your community, no doubt it has many of those attributes. But community also lives “in the small, repeated contacts of daily life—the neighbor who waves every morning, the co-worker who checks in when you seem off, the person at the coffee shop who remembers your order,” says Lucy Rose, the founder of The Cost of Loneliness Project, who is on a mission to combat loneliness and build human connection. The way she sees it, community “is the web of relationships where people feel seen and know they matter.”
Since 2017, we’ve conducted an annual search for the Nicest Places in America, highlighting amazing hometowns (and even a few individual businesses) that celebrate the idea of community as not just a place to live and work, but somewhere you really feel part of the broader whole. We’ve had some incredible winners over the last 10 years, and to commemorate this milestone anniversary, we thought we’d help you make your community the very best it can be. We talked to Rose, as well as Spud Marshall, founder of My Creative Community and the author of Designing Creative Communities, to learn tangible tips for making your hometown an even nicer place to live. We also checked in with Laura Malcolm, founder of Give InKind, to find out the best ways to respond in a crisis. Here’s how to strengthen your own community and create a place you can truly call home. Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more community building, cleaning, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long. “The answer changes from person to person—a new parent, a retiree and a 22-year-old need very different things from the same town,” Marshall says. But we can start with a few basics. “Safety, services and green space matter, and they create the conditions where connection can grow,” Rose says. “So do the places where people naturally gather: accessible sports leagues, arts events, the local restaurant that turns into an unofficial neighborhood hangout.”
But the idea of a nice place to live goes beyond things to do. “What ties all of those together is whether people walk away feeling like they belong,” Rose says. “What I hear again and again in my work is that people remember how a place made them feel more than what it offered them.”
Often, that comes down to finding human connection. Marshall says what sets a nice place apart is the “density of weak ties—the number of people you may recognize but don’t (yet) know well.” It’s these casual acquaintances that connect you to the broader whole. “The social-capital research backs this up, and honestly, you can feel it just walking down a street.”
Marshall even has a test: “How many places in your town can you go alone and reliably run into someone you know? That number tells you more than any ‘best places to live’ ranking.”
It’s as active as you want it to be. Nice places to live don’t just spring up out of nowhere, so the more you put in, the more you get out. But being active doesn’t have to mean joining a club or signing up for a long-term commitment. “Real impact often comes without any formal structure at all,” Rose says. “Checking on an elderly neighbor after a storm counts. So does inviting a new co-worker to lunch, or holding the door and actually asking someone how their day is going, then waiting for the real answer.”
Of course, if you want to get involved more formally, that’s great too. But don’t overlook the active participation of just being there for someone. “Those gestures matter more to the person on the receiving end than most of us realize, and they add up when people make a habit of noticing instead of waiting for a program to organize it for them,” Rose says. “Start with proximity,” Rose says. Look at what you’re already doing and go from there. “Here’s what most people miss: You already belong to more communities than you realize,” Marshall says. “The dog park at 7 a.m., the same grocery checkout line, the parents at daycare pickup.” It’s easier than you think. “The work isn’t finding community,” Marshall explains. “It’s noticing the communities you’re already in and adding one ounce of intention into them.”
Here are some expert-approved, tangible ways you can strengthen your community right now. If one doesn’t speak to you, try the next one. “The best option is the one that fits naturally into the life you’re already living,” Rose says. This one might be daunting, but it’s worth it. “Introduce yourself to a neighbor you haven’t met,” Rose says. You don’t have to go knock on their door or anything—just take a lap around the block a few nights a week. When you pass someone doing yard work or sitting on their porch, instead of looking at your phone or keeping your earbuds in, look up and say hi, along with your name. Most people will respond in kind. “Warm, attentive neighbors can make a town with modest amenities feel like home,” Rose says. No matter what size town you live in, there’s probably a local gathering going on sometime in the near future. It could be a library book fair, a church potluck or a local band playing down at the corner bar. Look on community message boards for events that sound fun to you. You don’t have to know anyone there, Rose says: “Show up to a local event, even if you’re going alone.” If that makes you nervous, remember that everyone else is there for the same reason: to enjoy a nice evening under the stars, find a book to read or support the same charity. If you meet someone, great. If you go home feeling that you’re not alone in this world, even better. “Host the low-bar thing, not the big thing,” Marshall says. “My wife and I host potluck brainstorms at our house with the simple goal of inviting strangers together to dream up new ways of making a difference in their town.” If you’re not sure how to get strangers on board, start with people you know and ask them to bring a friend. Who knows? Your small event could turn into something more. “The fun part is that [our] informal gathering turned into a series of formal groups over the years,” Marshall says. “And many of those groups have gone on to create significant impacts in our community.”
The simple act of putting your current group into new situations can foster community. “I also run kayak meetings and frisbee golf meetings instead of coffee, because doing something side by side is what lets people talk about the real stuff,” Marshall says. “It feels more real and memorable but doesn’t require joining a formal group of any sort.”
Is there an issue that’s close to your heart? “Volunteer somewhere that puts you face-to-face with people,” Rose says. This could be walking dogs at the animal shelter, sorting donated food or clothing at your church or a local shelter, or signing up to drive your neighbors to vote. Having a task keeps you busy, so you’ll feel less pressure to make small talk (though you’ll be surprised how easily conversations will come), and you’ll foster community while you’re at it. Marshall says building community is all about making small moves. You don’t have to spend every Saturday at the soup kitchen to make a difference. “Learn and actually use the names of five neighbors,” Marshall says. Once you know them, you can be the conduit for other connections. “Be the person who introduces two other people—a connector builds community without ever running anything.”
“Another important starting point is to say yes to the invitation you’d normally decline,” Marshall says. Do you always say “no” when your friend asks you to go hiking or play pickleball? Next time, change up your answer. “You’d be surprised where that ‘yes’ may lead you.”
It might seem strange to think about building community during a crisis, but it’s in these tough times that people come together. “Crisis tends to strip away the usual social distance between people, and that’s actually an opening,” Rose says. “When needs are acute, your direct presence and attention can matter as much as any supplies you bring.”
Here’s what you can do to help your community in a crisis. If the immediate crisis has spared you, offer to either check in with a point person or be that point of contact for your community, Malcolm says. If you can, organize a meal train, offer to set up a donation page, rally neighbors for support, or give your neighbor a call and just ask: “Hey, neighbor, this crisis is happening. Can I be the point of contact?”
Malcolm’s organization, Give InKind, hosts donation pages for people going through tough times. “You can take on setting up a page and find out exactly what’s needed, and people can come on and give support in those different ways that can be helpful,” she says. When natural disasters and other emergencies happen, we tend to look inward because the immediate needs are so acute. But don’t forget your neighbors, whether that’s the elderly man who just lost his wife or a person with special needs who might be frightened by the commotion. “Check on people who live alone,” Rose says. “That’s a really big one,” Malcolm agrees. Also remember that crises take many forms, not just tornadoes and hurricanes. “We have seniors who check themselves out of the hospital AMA [against medical advice] because there’s no one there to walk their dog.”
When things start getting back to normal, “stay in contact after the initial crisis passes, because that’s often when the isolation sets in hardest, once everyone else’s attention has moved on,” Rose says. Helping your neighbors will take different forms depending on the crisis. “If their house burned down, it might be gift cards for Airbnb or Home Depot,” Malcolm says. “If they have a child in the hospital, it might be that they need meals dropped off every night at a certain time for when they get home.”
Instead of asking generally what people need, Malcolm says it’s better to offer specific help. “Look for a thing that you know you can do, and offer to do it,” she says. “Say, ‘I’ll be responsible for wheeling your bins to the curb every week for the next six weeks unless you let me know otherwise.'”
Or if you’re organizing a meal train for someone, you might say, “We’re putting a cooler on your step, and we’ll let people know that if they’re dropping off meals, they should put them in the cooler between 5 and 6,” Malcolm says. “Let us know whether you want visitors.”
For you and me, it might be hard to single out one thing to do every day. But Rose and Marshall had answers immediately, and they were surprisingly aligned. “Be the one who says hello first,” Marshall says. “It sounds too small to matter, but it’s the whole ballgame–every relationship in your town starts with one person deciding not to look at their phone.” Or take it one step further: “Give away one specific useful thing a day: an introduction, a recommendation, a ride, 10 minutes of what you know.”
As for Rose? “Notice someone. Make eye contact, ask a real question, and listen to the answer,” she says. “It doesn’t take much time, but it’s also rare. Most people move through their day surrounded by others and still feel unseen.

“真诚的关注，哪怕只是短短一秒，就能打破某人的茧，而这并不需要任何代价。”

articles.title: Is It Really Rude to Not Tell Someone You’re Sick Before You Meet Up?
articles.content:
孩子突然对着我母亲喊道："妈，我的喉咙像吞下了刀片，还被浇上汽油点燃了。"接着，我的孩子做了孩子们常做的事——在我脸上咳嗽。当时距离我们计划飞往另一个州度假，去看久未谋面的亲人，只有一周时间。我感到她的飞沫溅到脸上时就知道，我们都完了——她、我、全家人，还有我们要拜访的亲友，甚至可能还有公众。

也许我早该预见到这一点。这是开学第一周，开学季简直等同于流感季。果然，两天后，我的喉咙也像吞下了刀片，被汽油浇灌后点燃一样疼痛。（她虽然夸张，但并非毫无道理。）不过，我至少没有对着别人咳嗽。

我们该怎么办？

感冒流感季节带来了一个礼仪难题，因为生病既不是社会性过错，也不是道德失败，这只是人类普遍经历。有时你直到站在别人厨房时才发现自己生病了。或者，你将偶尔的疲劳与鼻塞归咎于不过是疲惫。这完全可能是无关紧要的小问题。不过，感冒和流感之间存在巨大差异，前者可能在活动中途出现，而后者则是明知自己严重生病却还出现在四小时的室内派对上。

那么，如果感到自己可能要生病或确实生病了，最礼貌的做法是什么？不提前告诉别人你生病了，真的很失礼吗？拿一包纸巾，让我们来讨论一下。

告诉别人你生病了，本质上是给他们做决定所需的信息。你的传染性状况对健康人士很重要，但对那些必须避免生病的人更为重要，比如孕妇、老人、幼儿或免疫力低下者。不告知他们可能会带来严重后果。这也是非常重要的信息，对于那些正在准备重要活动的人来说，比如婚礼、度假或手术。而且，你可能并不知道这些情况，因为人们通常不会提前说明自己不能生病的理由。

还有实际原因需要分享：你可能看起来确实生病了。如果你两个口袋里都塞满了纸巾，声音像艾尔·帕西诺一样，别人一定会察觉到什么不对劲。当他们知道你明知生病却不告诉他们时，可能会感到至少是挫败，最糟是背叛。

当然，我们确实需要提到那些对细菌恐惧症患者的朋友（你私下认为他们有点过分）。确实有不告诉他们的诱惑，因为他们可能会大惊小怪，但我认为这正是你应该告诉他们的理由。焦虑常常源于缺乏信息。你坦率诚实的态度可以帮助消除他们的恐惧。或者他们会取消约会，但这是他们的决定。

关键区别在于，告诉别人你生病并不等于请求允许。你可以说："嗨，我今天早上感冒了，想在见面前告诉你。完全理解如果你想改期的话。"这样，他们就有了信息，可以决定自己觉得合适的做法。

也有不把每次打喷嚏都当成紧急情况的道理。有时候，额外的信息只会带来额外的压力，尤其是对那些本就担心生病的人。感冒在流感季很常见。告诉别人你在感冒季有点感冒并不令人惊讶或独特。毕竟，几乎所有人都在流鼻涕，出门后也会处处打喷嚏。

更何况，人们并不总是知道自己是否具有传染性。你可能清晨感觉完全正常，度过一天后晚上才发现喉咙痛。可能你的流鼻涕只是过敏。或者，你有一个持续三周的咳嗽余症，已不再具有传染性。我们都有过这样的日子，感觉比平时更疲惫，不知道是否是疾病的前兆，还是因为边看《肖申克的救赎》边吃太多甜甜圈。（最后一点可能只是我。）无论如何，期望每次社交场合前都自我诊断正确，要求实在太高。

而且，别人真的需要这些信息吗？隐私如今正在迅速消失，我们应该紧紧抓住剩下的每一丝碎片，即使这些碎片存在于我们的窦腔中。此外，对于那些过于分享的人来说，感觉需要报告所有症状可能是一种可怕的过度分享——尤其是牵扯到腰部以下的任何内容。人们并不想要或需要你的如厕详细记录。

当然，关于是否要提前告诉别人你生病了的最佳礼仪建议是……视情况而定。取决于什么？

一个并不模糊的灰色地带：既然你已经承诺，就必须去，无论怎样。有些人认为取消比生病出现更糟，因为"我已经答应去了"。但大多数主人更希望避免接触传染源，或者至少提前知晓。

简单即是关键。他们不需要医学论文。可以这样说："只是想提醒你，我今天早上感冒了。我感觉还不错，但想在见面前告诉你。完全理解如果你想改期的话。"

如果不确定自己是否真正生病："我今天喉咙有点发痒，不确定是否要感冒了。其他方面感觉还行，但想提前告诉你。"

如果明确知道自己确实生病了："你好，朋友。我确实生病了，所以觉得我们应该改期。抱歉，我本来很期待见到你。"

注意，这三条信息都没有给对方施加压力。你也没有说这不算大事，对方不需要担心。给他们信息，让他们自己决定。

该是你做个人风险评估的时候了。当然，这会因人而异。如果你有任何不适，完全可以要求改变计划——比如改在户外活动——或者道歉离开。不需要大张旗鼓地宣布或指责对方不负责任。

"我正努力避免生病。不介意改期吗？"这样很好。

取消行程似乎不是选项——这趟访问太重要了。我女儿和我都没有特别严重的病症（我们的COVID和流感检测均为阴性），参与者中也没有老人或免疫力低下者。但丈夫和我一致认为，我们需要在到达前告诉家人。他们并不高兴，但仍然希望我们来。于是，我们在飞机上和公共区域戴着口罩，住在酒店而非他们的家中，并将许多活动改为户外。

你知道吗？这趟行程最终非常棒。所有人都玩得很开心，大部分原因是没有人对我们生病感到意外。

是的，不提前告诉别人你生病了是很礼貌的……如果你的疾病可能合理改变别人是否想见你的话。并非所有情况都需要披露，但作为一般原则，这是值得分享的信息。如果他们选择改期，不要介意。如果他们仍想见你，尽量减少传染风险。如果明知自己病得很重，或者要接触特别脆弱的人群，考虑取消或改变计划，而非让别人因你而陷入不得不决定的尴尬境地。

礼仪并非关于你是否生病，而是提供足够信息让别人决定是否愿意与你和你带来的微生物共度一个下午。

至于我女儿"喉咙像吞下刀片并点燃"的抱怨？我们都康复了，家人顺利完成了行程，没有人生病。这说明有时一点诚实、几个预防措施和对他人肺部的健康尊重能起到很好的作用。虽然我认为"我的喉咙像吞下刀片并点燃了"不过是索要冰棍的复杂说法罢了。

“Mom? My throat feels like I swallowed razor blades, doused them in gasoline and lit them on fire.” Then my dramatic child did what children do and coughed right in my face. It was one week before we were set to fly for a much-anticipated vacation in another state to visit family members we hadn’t seen in forever. As soon as I felt the droplets hit my face, I knew we were all doomed—her, me, the rest of the family, the folks we were visiting and maybe some of the general public. 

I probably should have seen it coming. It was the first week of school, and back-to-school might as well be called back-to-flu. And sure enough, two days later, my throat also felt like I swallowed razor blades, doused them in gasoline and set them on fire. (She may have been dramatic, but she wasn’t wrong.) I did, however, manage to refrain from coughing in anyone’s face. 

What should we do? 

Cold and flu season creates an etiquette dilemma because getting sick isn’t a social offense or a moral failing. It’s just human. And sometimes you don’t know you’re sick until you’re already standing in someone else’s kitchen. Or you attribute feeling a little fatigued or sniffly to just being, well, a little fatigued. It literally could be nothing. That being said, there’s a big a difference between coming down with the sniffles mid-event and knowingly showing up to a four-hour indoor party while hacking up a lung like consumption is in vogue again.

So what is the polite thing to do if you feel like you’re coming down with something or you’re flat-out sick? Is it really rude to not tell someone you’re sick before you meet up? Grab a box of tissues, and let’s discuss. 

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

The case for telling them you’re sick

Telling people you’re sick is simply about giving them the information they need to make the decision that’s best for them. Your infectious status is important info for regular healthy people, but it’s even more important for people who really need to avoid getting sick, like people who are pregnant, very old, very young or immunocompromised. Not telling them could have terrible consequences. It is also very pertinent info for people who may be preparing for an important event like a wedding, vacation or surgery. And you likely don’t know all of those circumstances because people don’t usually preemptively announce what they can’t get sick for. 

There’s a practical reason to share as well: You probably look sick. If you show up with two pockets stuffed full of tissues and a voice like Al Pacino, they’re going to know something is up. Realizing that you knew you were sick and didn’t say anything may feel like a frustration, at best, and a betrayal, at worst. 

Of course, we do need to mention the friend who’s a germophobe (and you privately think is being a little ridiculous). There’s a definite temptation not to tell them because they’ll turn it into A Big Thing, but I’d say that’s even more of a reason to let them know. Anxiety often stems from a lack of information. You being matter-of-fact and honest can help allay their fears. Or they’ll cancel, but that’s their decision to make.

The important distinction here is that telling someone you’re sick isn’t the same as asking for permission. You can say, “Hey, I woke up with a head cold, and I just wanted to let you know before we met up. Totally get it if you’d rather reschedule.” Boom, done. Now they have the information, and they can decide what they feel good about doing.

The case for not telling them

There are also good reasons for not turning every sneeze into an emergency alert. Sometimes, extra information just causes extra stress, especially for people already prone to worrying about getting sick. Colds are endemic. Telling someone you have a little cold during cold season isn’t particularly surprising or unique. After all, nearly everyone is sniffling then, and they’ll be sniffling and sneezing all around you when you’re out.

Not to mention that people don’t always know when they’re contagious. You can wake up feeling completely normal, go through your day and realize at night that you have a sore throat. Maybe your sniffly nose is just allergies. Or you have a lingering cough from a cold three weeks ago that’s no longer contagious. And we’ve all had those days when we feel more tired than usual and wonder if it’s the onset of an illness or just too many churros while binge-watching The Pitt. (That last one might just be me.) At any rate, expecting someone to diagnose themselves correctly before every social occasion is a pretty high bar.

And do others really need that info about you? Privacy is a swiftly dwindling resource these days, and we should hold on to the few shreds we have left, even if those shreds are in our sinuses. Plus, for people who tend to disclose too much, feeling like you need to report all your symptoms can be a terrible type of oversharing—especially if it involves anything below the waist. People don’t want or need the play-by-play of your bathroom adventures. 

The gray areas

Of course, the best etiquette advice about whether or not to tell someone you’re sick before you meet up is … it depends. On what?

  • The location. Are you going to an outdoor baseball game where all those germs will get diluted in the stadium, not to mention be in a place with a whole bunch of other people harboring their own viruses? Or are you going to someone’s house, where you’ll breathe the same air for three hours?
  • The event. Is this a family gathering where great-grandparents and babies will be? Or are you playing frisbee in the park with friends?
  • The illness. A mild head cold is a far cry from the flu, COVID or something that requires both a garbage can and a toilet. One is a small annoyance, and the others can take people out for days—and are super contagious.
  • The sick person. The dynamics change when it’s a child who is sick. Kids get sick far more often than adults, and they are not particularly hygienic or cooperative about not sneezing in other people’s eyeballs. As a parent of a sick child, you need to be open about their contagiousness too.
  • Steps you are willing to take. Are you willing to mask up? Bring extra hand sanitizer? Be flexible about the location and activity? Taking responsibility for what you can control and doing your best to ameliorate that risk goes a long way in relationships.

One gray area that isn’t so gray: the idea that you already committed, so you have to go, no matter what. People sometimes feel that canceling is worse than showing up sick because “I said I’d be there.” But most hosts would rather avoid germ exposure or at least be given a heads-up about it.

So what should you actually say?

Just keep it simple. They don’t need to send a medical dissertation. Something like: “Just a heads-up that I woke up with a cold today. I’m feeling OK, but I wanted you to know before we got together. Totally understand if you’d rather reschedule.”

Or if you’re not sure whether you’re actually sick: “I have a scratchy throat today, and I’m not sure if I’m coming down with something. I feel fine otherwise, but I wanted to give you a heads-up.”

Or if you know you’re genuinely sick: “Hey, friend. I’m definitely sick, so I think we should reschedule. I’m sorry. I was really looking forward to seeing you.”

Notice that all three messages avoid pressuring the other person. You’re also not saying that it’s not a big deal and the other person shouldn’t worry about it. Give them the information, and let them decide.

What if you’re the one who shows up and discovers someone is sick?

Time to make your own personal-risk calculation. Of course, that will look different for each person. If you’re uncomfortable for any reason, it’s perfectly fine to ask to change plans—like moving things outside—or excuse yourself. No need to make a dramatic announcement or accuse them of being irresponsible.

“I’m actually trying really hard not to get sick right now. Would you mind if we reschedule?” is great.

So what happened with our trip?

Canceling the trip didn’t feel like an option—the visit was too important. Neither my daughter nor I had a particularly serious illness (we tested negative for both COVID and the flu), and no one involved was elderly or immunocompromised. But my husband and I agreed that we needed to tell our family before we showed up. They weren’t thrilled, but they still wanted us to come. So we wore masks on the airplane and in common areas, stayed in a hotel instead of their house and changed several of our activities to be outdoors.

And you know what? The trip turned out great. Everyone had a wonderful time, in large part because nobody was surprised when we showed up sick.

The verdict

Yes, it’s rude not to tell someone you’re sick before you meet up … if your illness could reasonably change whether someone wants to see you. Not every circumstance will require a disclosure, but as a general rule of thumb, this is information that’s polite to share. If they opt to reschedule, don’t take it personally. But if they want to see you anyway, do your best to minimize germ exposure. And if you know you’re sick sick—or you’re going to be around people who are especially vulnerable—consider canceling or changing the plans rather than putting others in the uncomfortable position of deciding for you.

The etiquette isn’t about whether you got sick; it’s about giving people enough information to decide whether they want to spend the afternoon with you and whatever microscopic hitchhikers you’ve brought along.

As for my daughter’s razor-blades-on-fire throat? We both recovered, our family survived the trip, and nobody else got sick. Which proves that sometimes a little honesty, a few precautions and a healthy respect for other people’s lungs can go a long way. Although I still maintain that “my throat feels like I swallowed razor blades and lit them on fire” was an unnecessarily elaborate way to ask for a popsicle.
